carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: f the Proto‐Tethys Ocean. However, until now, only two Early Paleozoic paleomagnetic results are available for the OT. The paleomagnetic results reported by Yang et al. ( 1992 ) indicate that the Early Ordovician paleolatitude for the OT was ∼ 13°S; however, their Early Ordovician paleomagnetic results are derived from only 10 samples and they lack field tests. A new Early Ordovician paleomagnetic result was recently reported by Cao et al. ( 2021 ). This result also lacked field tests, but the characteristic remanent magnetizations are all reverse polarities and are consistent with the Moyero Reversed Polarity Superchron, which indicates the primary origin of the characteristic remanence. This result indicates that the OT was located at a low latitude near the equator during the Early Ordovician (Cao et al., 2021 ). Here we report the first Late Cambrian paleomagnetic results for the OT. These paleomagnetic results, combined with geological evidence, provide reliable constraints on the paleogeographic affinity of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau, and the paleogeography of the Proto‐Tethys Ocean during the Late Cambrian. 2. As mentioned above, the paleogeographic position of the OT during the Late Cambrian inferred from the new paleomagnetic results is consistent with the sedimentological evidence. 4.2. Late Cambrian Paleogeography of the Proto‐Tethys Ocean During the Late Cambrian, the main body of the Gondwana continent was assembled in the Southern Hemisphere; Laurentia was located at low equatorial latitudes; Baltica was located at ∼ 40–70°S; and Siberia was located between 30°S and the equator (Torsvik et al., 2012 ). The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) reported by Huang et al. ( 2018 ) suggests that the North China, South China, and Tarim blocks were located within 30° of the equator in the Southern Hemisphere during the Late Cambrian. The three blocks were located on the western margin of East Gondwana (Huang et al., 2018 ). The SCB may have been part of Gondwana and connected to the northwestern margin of Australia during the Late Cambrian (Li et al., 2018 ; Yang et al., 2004 ). The Lhasa, Qiangtang, and Indochina terranes were collectively located at the Gondwana margin during the Early Paleozoic (Metcalfe, 2011 ). Plain Language Summary The Proto‐Tethys Ocean underwent a complex process of collision and amalgamation of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau during the Early Paleozoic. Unraveling the Early Paleozoic paleogeography of these terranes is important for understanding the evolution of the Proto‐Tethys Ocean and is critical for reconstructing the formation of East Asia. However, quantitative constraints on the Early Paleozoic paleogeographic position of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau are limited. Paleomagnetism is the only effective approach for directly constraining the paleolatitude of terranes. We conducted a paleomagnetic study of the Late Cambrian strata in the Oulongbuluke terrane (OT), northern Tibetan Plateau. The results define the paleolatitude of 20.6 ± 4.6 °S for the OT during the Late Cambrian. Nonetheless, the ages of the basins are controversial because of the discordance between radiometric dating results and paleontological ages. Despite possible remagnetization, the dual‐polarity magnetization, hosted in different minerals and lithologies, likely represents a middle Permian remanence. This constraint implies the Lhasa Block was located at 16.7 ± 5.3°S at 267.8 ± 5 Ma, following its rifting from Gondwana. Geological Setting and Sampling Upper Paleozoic strata are widely distributed in the Lhasa Block. Upper Carboniferous–lower Permian strata are characterized by glaciomarine diamictites that were then common across large areas of Gondwana, whereas middle to upper Permian strata are mainly distributed in the central part of the Lhasa Block, where they are characterized by marine sedimentary rocks, locally interbedded with volcanics (Figure 1a ). The latter include an early (middle Permian) phase of basaltic volcanism and a later (middle to late Permian) phase of intermediate to silicic volcanism (Geng et al., 2009 ). The most extensive exposure of the older volcanic phase, referred to as the Luobadui Formation, is located north of Luobadui village, Chundui Township, Lhunzhub County (Geng et al., 2009 ). The Luobadui Formation consists of a volcano‐sedimentary sequence, including marine carbonates and sandstones, interspersed with volcanic layers of basalt, basaltic breccia, tuff, and andesite. All 1575 ChRM directions, together with the calculated paleolatitudes of the virtual geomag- netic poles, were used to construct the final mag- netic polarity sequence of the Mangang, Jing- xing, and Bazhulu formations in the JC section. Each magnetozone was defined by at least two (usually more) consecutive stratigraphic levels with the same polarity. A total of 25 normal (N7– N31) and 25 reversed (R8–R32) polarity zones were detected (Figs. 8A–8G); these zones were labeled following the previous scheme (N1–N6 and R1–R7) of the Mengyejing Formation (Yan et al., 2021a) in the upper JC section for compre- hensive and intuitive presentation. The obtained 25 normal and 25 reversed polarity zones are characterized by a long normal polarity domi - nant zone (N7–N10) for the Mangang Formation

Laboratory techniques In the laboratory, the samples were cut into 2.2-cm-long cylinders for subsequent paleomagnetic analysis. All samples underwent stepwise thermal demagnetization up to 580 °C, performed with an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer with an internal residual ﬁeld of < 10 nT. Demagnetization temperature intervals were generally large (40 –60 °C) in the low temperature part, and smaller (20 –30 °C) at higher tem- peratures. Remanent magnetizations were measured using a 2G-755R cryogenic magnetometer. In order to identify the magnetic minerals, stepwise thermal demagnetization of a three-component isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) were measured using a JR-6 spinner magnetometer. It is separated from the Tarim Block by the Altyn Tagh fault zone to the north, from the Songpan- Ganze Block by the East Kunlun fault zone to the southeast, and from the Kunlun Block by the Qimen Tagh fault zone to the south ( Fig. 1 b). Strata outcrops in the Qaidam Basin are mainly Cenozoic sediments. Outcrops of Pre-Cenozoic strata are limited to the western and northern margins, and outcrops of Carboniferous strata are limited to the basin margin. Major Upper Carboniferous deposits in the Qaidam Basin in- clude the Zhongwunongshan Group (C 2zh), the Zhabusagaxiu Forma- tion (C 2z) and Keluke Formation (C 2k). Lower Carboniferous deposits include the Huaitoutala Formation (C 1h) and Chengqianggou Formation (C1c). In the study area, outcropping rocks consist mainly of Paleozoic and Proterozoic strata ( Fig. 1c). Examples are the Cambrian Ou- longbuluke Formation, Ordovician Duoquanshan Formation, Lower Carboniferous Huaitoutala Formation, Upper Carboniferous Keluke Formation and Upper Carboniferous Zhabusagaxiu Formation. There are several NW-SE faults and left-lateral strike-slip faults in the study area ( Fig. 1c). The sampled locality lies at the northern margin of the Qaidam Block (Fig. 1). Late Carboniferous Zhabusagaxiu Formation. It is separated from the Tarim Block by the Altyn Tagh fault zone to the north, from the Songpan- Ganze Block by the East Kunlun fault zone to the southeast, and from the Kunlun Block by the Qimen Tagh fault zone to the south ( Fig. 1 b). Strata outcrops in the Qaidam Basin are mainly Cenozoic sediments. Outcrops of Pre-Cenozoic strata are limited to the western and northern margins, and outcrops of Carboniferous strata are limited to the basin margin. Major Upper Carboniferous deposits in the Qaidam Basin in- clude the Zhongwunongshan Group (C 2zh), the Zhabusagaxiu Forma- tion (C 2z) and Keluke Formation (C 2k). Lower Carboniferous deposits include the Huaitoutala Formation (C 1h) and Chengqianggou Formation (C1c). In the study area, outcropping rocks consist mainly of Paleozoic and Proterozoic strata ( Fig. 1c). Courtillot Abstract We have carried out a detailed magnetostratigraphic study of Tertiary sediments in the northern margin of the Qaidam Basin, northern Tibetan plateau. A total of 400 paleomagnetic samples (with an interval of about 2 m) were collected from the Shanggancaigou and Xiagancaigou Formations in the Hongsanhan section. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. These, mainly Cenozoic, prograding sedimentary profiles are fairly monotonous throughout the region. The basal parts of the sequences are mainly fine-grained and represent deposition centers lying at some distance from the uplifting mountains. When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. Paleomagnetic constraints on the amount of displacement along the Altyn Tagh fault are difficult to establish because the fault’s easterly strike would require thousands of kilometers of offset in order to be resolvable by paleolatitude differences. One way around this problem is to use paleomagnetic rotations. First, if the Qaidam Basin rotated relative to the Tarim Basin, the relative motion must be mostly taken up by slip along the Altyn Tagh fault. Second, one can sample time- progressive sequences to determine when (or if) a partic- ular block had (or had not) rotated. A paleomagnetic study along the Altyn Tagh fault by Rumelhar

zes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. Here again considerable overlap likely exists in time, which most probably leads to age uncertainties larger than those for the Cenozoic. Exceptions are in the western part of the Tarim Basin (and also in the Lhasa block) where fossiliferous Cretaceous and Paleogene marine carbonates crop out within the red bed sequences. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. These, mainly Cenozoic, prograding sedimentary profiles are fairly monotonous throughout the region. The basal parts of the sequences are mainly fine-grained and represent deposition centers lying at some distance from the uplifting mountains. When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. These, mainly Cenozoic, prograding sedimentary profiles are fairly monotonous throughout the region. First, if the Qaidam Basin rotated relative to the Tarim Basin, the relative motion must be mostly taken up by slip along the Altyn Tagh fault. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. Introduction Large igneous provinces (LIPs) are magmatic provinces that cover areas greater than 100,000 km 2, contain igneous volumes exceeding 100,000 km 3, and are usually characterized by an intense eruptive pulse(s) of short duration ( –5 Myr)

al rela- tionship with the KMP. Considering that (1) some published latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the TH lack robust ﬁeld tests to question the reliability of the data ( Klootwijk and Bingham, 1980; Zhu et al., 1981; Patzelt et al., 1996; Li et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2015 ); and (2) although these Jurassic and Cre- taceous igneous rocks have an overall similarity in geochemical characteristics to the KMP (e.g., Zhu et al., 2007, 2008; Shi et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022 ), the spatial relationship of these latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous igneous rocks to the KMP is an essential prerequisite for understanding the causal link between the eastern Gondwana breakup and the KMP, additional reliable latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data- sets with well-established ages constraint from the TH are still required to address the aforementioned issues. In this study, we present an analysis of paleomagnetic data on the Zhela Formation (Fm.) basalts and sandstones in the Taga area of the eastern TH. The new results allow us to constrain the pale- ogeography of the TH during the latest Jurassic to Early Cretaceous and thus provide a better understanding of the causal link between the CBLIP and the KMP. 2. Introduction The geomagnetic field, produced by thermo-chemical convection of an electrically conducting fluid in Earth's outer core, experienced significant changes in its rate of polarity reversals throughout geologic times. In particular, two end-member polarity regimes have been identified during the Phanerozoic (e.g., Gallet & Pavlov, 2016). On the one hand, three superchrons—the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (CNS, 84–121 Ma), the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (267–318 Ma) and the Ordovician Reverse Superchron (463–485 Ma)—are defined as prolonged periods with stable polarity (e.g., Ogg, 2020; Pavlov & Gallet, 2005). On the other, two hyperactivity events, with more than 10 reversals per million year, were hypothesized during the Middle Jurassic (155–171 Ma; e.g., Tivey et al., 2006; Tominaga et al., 2008

geomagnetic field can also experience fluctuations in its average intensity F and its spatiotemporal variability during stable periods (termed hereafter paleosecular variation, PSV). To better characterize the paleosecular variation (PSV) of the geomagnetic field at the end of this interval, we sampled seven continuous sequences of lava flows from the Okhotsk-Chukotka Volcanic Belt, emplaced 84–89 Ma in the vicinity of the Kupol ore deposit (NE Russia). From a collection of 1,024 paleomagnetic cores out of 82 investigated lava flows, we successfully determined the paleodirections of 78 lava flows, which led to 57 directional groups after removing the serial correlations. Most VGPs remain in the northern hemisphere (positive latitudes) at high latitudes ( > 60 ◦ ), with a few migrating to the southern hemisphere but only reaching medium lati - tudes, compatible with an excursion and not a complete reversal of the geomagnetic field. However, at the base of sections 1 to 3 , the variability of the VGPs suggests a recovering field from a reversal. The topmost sections, 6 and 7, exhibit different behavior than the others, with their VGPs at medium latitudes in the base and a complete reversal on the top of the sequences between elevations 772 – 774 m. The reversed magne - tization component is of primary origin and remains stable during de - magnetizations up to 80 mT or 600 ◦ C. This reversed field was probably imparted as a soft secondary component in a few samples of sections 1 and 2 , as mentioned before and seen in Figs. 3 and 5 . On the stereogram of Fig. 8 , the distribution of the VGPs calculated after the inclination correction shows a tight cluster near the geographic pole corresponding mainly to the results from sections 1 to 5 and a higher dispersion of data from sections 6 and 7. Notably, the Uberaba Formation, which occupies a restricted area in the northeastern portion of the basin ( Fig. 1 ), is in contact with the Serra Geral basalts. Despite this, its depositional characteristics indicate contributions from the Late Cretaceous Alto Paranaiba alkaline volcanism to the north ( Ferreira Júnior and Gomes, 1999 ). Previous magnetostratigraphic research on the Uberaba Formation placed it in the Campanian-Maastrichtian ( Tamrat et al., 2002 ), and the authors identified some polarity intervals loosely correlated with the geomagnetic polarity time scale. However, the rough data was never fully published, and no paleomagnetic pole was calculated. n the Bauru Group, was deposited over the Early Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the Paran ´a Basin in southern Brazil. It occupies a restricted northeastern area of the basin surrounding the homonymous city. Recent works on stratigraphy and paleontology indicate a Campanian age, a novel finding that challenges the previously held belief of a Cenomanian age based on dinosaur bones. Paleomagnetic work on seven sections of the Uberaba formation has resulted in the calculation of a paleo - magnetic pole at 82.2 ◦ S 350.8 ◦ E (N = 89; k = 23; A 95 = 3.2 ◦ ) after correcting for the shallowing of the magnetic inclination caused by overload. The formation is dated to ~73 Ma (Campanian) age based on magnetostrati - graphic data and comparisons with other Late Cretaceous poles. The area stayed as a highland until the tectonic events related to the northward emplacement of the alkaline provinces. (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). To the south of the Lhasa terrane, the IYS features Xigaze forearc basin (XFB) and the Xigaze accretionary complex, which include ophiolites and m ´elanges ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Stretching more than 500 km from Renbu in the east to Zhongba in the west, the XFB extends along the Yarlung Zangbo River in an east – west orientation ( Wang et al., 2012 ). Isolated remnants of forearc sediments are sporadically found in the Zanda area ( Sun et al., 2018 ). The XFB, dating from the Early Cretaceous to the Eocene, is exposed as an east – west trending syncline with a westward inclination ( Metcalf and Kapp, 2019 ). 230 samples underwent thermal demagnetization processes. (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). To the south of the Lhasa terrane, the IYS features Xigaze forearc basin (XFB) and the Xigaze accretionary complex, which include ophiolites and m ´elanges ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Stretching more than 500 km from Renbu in the east to Zhongba in the west, the XFB extends along the Yarlung Zangbo River in an east – west orientation ( Wang et al., 2012 ). Isolated remnants of forearc sediments are sporadically found in the Zanda area ( Sun et al., 2018 ). The XFB, dating from the Early Cretaceous to the Eocene, is exposed as an east – west trending syncline with a westward inclination ( Metcalf and Kapp, 2019 ). Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic results 4.1. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). At Backside Beck the red-samples from the Hebblethwaite Mbr, and some non-red samples from the Browgill Fm have > 80% of IRM acquisition above 200 mT and Hcr > 280 mT ( Fig. 9 a). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). The hard ferrimagnetic mineral in most of these sam - ples is haematite as shown by the resistance of the NRM to thermal demagnetisation (see later). Fig. 6. Detailed magnetic and organic matter car

Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. However, appreciable secondary magnetization persists in many samples, even after demag- netization up through either 645°C to 670°C. Stereographic projection of all demagnetized results is shown in Figure 3A. In summary, samples from twenty-two intervals display reversed polarity up to 580°C, and then dis- play Early Jurassic normal polarity at higher temperatures, typically at 645°C. Generally these samples display Jurassic normal polarity at only one demagnetization temperature, and return to reversed or intermediate directions in high tem- perature steps. Overall, the Kayenta Formation largely recorded re- versed polarity, but 9 to 11 short intervals present short nor- mal polarity intervals (Fig. 4). Sample acquisition, preparation, measurement and rock magnetic analysis 3.1. Acquisition, preparation, measurement and demagnetization All samples were obtained as oriented cores in the field using stan - dard methods. In the Pacific Northwest Paleomagnetism Laboratory at the Western Washington University, the 2.5 cm in diameters cores were sliced into specimens 2.2 cm in length. Remanent magnetization was measured with a 2G Enterprise model 755 three-axis DC-SQUID magnetometer in a magnetically shielded room, which has an internal field of less than 350 nT. Progressive thermal demagnetization was employed to reveal components of Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of specimens using the ASC model TD48 furnace. Progressive alternating field (a.f.) demagnetization used an ASC D-2000 unit with peak fields of 200 mT. A total of 345 specimens, 190 from Upper Triassic and 155 from Middle Jurassic formations, were demagnetized. Samples that were suspected to have magnetite as their main remanence carrier were demagnetized using a.f., which was generally ineffective, and at best a large p

rge portion of NRM (generally > 50%) remained after a.f. demagneti - zation. At least one specimen per layer was selected for pilot thermal demagnetization with temperature steps of 50 – 100 ◦ C below 500 ◦ C, 10 – 30 ◦ C between 500 ◦ and 630 ◦ or 650 ◦ C, and 3 – 10 ◦ C above 650 ◦ C. After this revealed the general demagnetization behavior of each set, most of the specimens were thermally cleaned at larger intervals below 500 ◦ C, 30 – 40 ◦ C steps up to 600 ◦ or 630 ◦ C, and very small steps (3 – 10 ◦ C) for temperatures above 630 ◦ C. In most samples, it appeared that hematite is the main carrier of the remanence, and unblocking temperature ranges above 650 ◦ C were used to reveal the Characteristic Remanent Magnetization (ChRM) compo - nent of specimens. Linear demagnetization paths (at high unblocking temperature ranges) were quantified with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of Kirschvink (1980) , while the great-circle (GC) fits ( McFadden and McElhinny, 1988 ) were employed for non-linear paths. To not bias directions by possible relatively high-temperature overprints, unan - chored line-fits were used for most specimens. The zone-mean paleomagnetic directions of raw and smoothed datasets are very similar with generally better precision for the smoothed version (see Table 2 ), which shows that smoothing did not bias the results and was beneficial to identify the ChRMs as it increased signal to noise ratio. 4.1.2. Site division Initially, the two or three samples from each sampled horizon were grouped as a site in the hope that each would provide a good average of the field at time of deposition. However, because most of the specimens had very noisy and non-linear demagnetization paths, the best approach seemed to be to group samples from adjacent horizons that preserved a single polarity zone. Each group defined in this way we call a ‘zone ’ ( Table 1 ). Thus, zone-mean directions come from a group of specimens from adjacent horizons that appeared to belong to a single polarity interval. 4.2. Institute of Geology, China Seismological Bureau, Beijing 100029, China Abstract Detailed rock magnetic studies of 55 lavas from Yixian and Fuxin area, West Liaoning, show the primary carriers of remanence to be pseudo-single domain ti- tanomagnetite. K/Ar dating indicates that the volcanic se- quence spans 93 to 133 Ma. Stepwise thermal demagnetiza- tion successfully isolated well-defined characteristic mag- netization (ChRM) in all lavas thermal-treated above 250 ć. The mean paleodirections are D/I = 5.9 /58.8 (D95 = 2.9 ) and D/I =179.2 /59.9 ( D95 = 5.2 ) for 27 normally magnetized flows and 28 reversibly magnetized flows, respectively. It indicates that since the Early Cretaceous there is no signifi- cant horizontal movement and

compression system to an expansion system. Meanwhile, in this region al so occurred both deep conti- nental subduction and the crust shortening [1]. Numerous metal deposits, oil and gas resources were accumulated, which is supposed to be closely related with the in- tra-continental tectonic processes since the Mesozoic. Therefore, investigations on continental tectonic history of eastern China are obviously very important for the study of continental dynamics. Th is note aims to study the kinematics characteristics of intracontinental blocks in eastern China since the Mesozoic by means of paleomag- netism. 1 Geological settings and sample collection Eastern China underwent frequent intensive volcanic eruptions resulting from a complex influence of the west- ern Pacific plate and deep Earth’s processes during the middle to late Mesozoic. The age of the Tiaojishan Formation volcanics was recently dated from 153 Ma to 161 Ma by U –Pb and 40Ar–39Ar. A total of 154 samples from 16 sites within the Tiaojishan Formation were collected. Detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization allows us to isolate two components from 77 oriented drill-core samples. A low-temperature component identi ﬁed in most samples falls close to the present local Earth ﬁeld direction. Characteristic remanent directions obtained from high-temperature pass-reversal test yield a pole position at 240.3°E, 59.9°N with α95 = 6.8°. Combined with coeval paleopoles obtained from the Siberia Block (SIB), these results show a signi ﬁcant paleolatitude displacement between the NCB and SIB, which indicates that the Mongol –Okhotsk Ocean was still open with ~ 3000 km width in its eastern part at ca. 155 Ma. © 2011 Elsevier B.V. The age of the Tiaojishan Formation volcanics was recently dated from 153 Ma to 161 Ma by U –Pb and 40Ar–39Ar. A total of 154 samples from 16 sites within the Tiaojishan Formation were collected. Geological setting and paleomagnetic sampling The Chengde basin is geologically located in the southern margin of the Yanshan Belt (YSB), itself located at the northern margin of the NCB ( Fig. 1 ; Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990 ). To the north, the Xing- Meng suture (Suolon suture) indicates a ﬁnal closure of the Paleo- Asian ocean and the collision between the NCB and AMU during the Permian (Badarch et al., 2002; Li, 2006; Xiao et al., 2004; Yin and Nie, 1996). The YSB experienced vertical movements accompanied by intense deformation during the Mesozoic, including multiple generations of folds, thrusts and extensional faults (Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990). In the Early Jurassic, a series of rift basins bounded by normal faulting were developed on the amalgamated NCB and AMU ( Darby et al., 2001; Meng, 2003; Zhao et al., 2002 ). From Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous, extensive terrestrial volcanic and clastic sediments were deposited in these fault-related rift basins. These volcanic rocks, varying from ma ﬁc to intermediate- acid in composition, were genetically related to the process of lithospheric replacement beneath the NCB ( Zhang et al., 2003 ). Key words: Mesozoic, North China Block, palaeomagnetism, tectonics. 1 INTRODUCTION The North China Block and the South China Block are the major tectonic blocks forming East Asia (Fig. 1). The two blocks were located in distinct positions from each other through Precambrian– Palaeozoic times and were welded through a collision process in Early Mesozoic times. The collision of the North and South China Blocks is recognized by metamorphic belts observed between the two blocks. The Dabie Belt and the Sulu Belt that bound the two blocks yield coesite-bearing ultrahigh-pressure metamorphic rocks (Okay & S¸ eng¨or 1992). The Tan-Lu Fault also marks the bound- ary between the North and South China Blocks. This fault, to the north of the Dabie Belt and to the south of the Sulu Belt, marks the biogeographical and lithological boundary between the two blocks (Kobayashi 1967). Permian and Early Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data sets from the North and South China Blocks suggest that the two blocks su- tured following a scissor-like collision process (Zhao & Coe 1987). The North and South China Blocks experienced counterclockwise and clockwise rotations during the welding event, respectively. The Nor

e North China Block with respect to the South China Block during the welding event. At present, the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic representa- tive poles for the North China Block are based on palaeomagnetic data from a small number of studies (Y ang et al. 1991, 1992) that come from a single locality within the block (Ordos Basin, Fig. 1). The palaeomagnetic data of these important time periods have not been improved over the last decade. Attempts to accumulate reliable Triassic and Jurassic data have been thwarted by remagnetizations and lack of outcrops with good structural conditions to perform fold tests. As seen in the Early Jurassic demagnetization results of Y anget al. (1992), even successful palaeomagnetic works have encountered difﬁculties in isolating a high-ﬁdelity record of geo- magnetic ﬁeld directions in the North China Block, and a further study needs to be undertaken in order to contribute toward establish- ing representative Triassic and Jurassic poles for the North China Block. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic results from Late Triassic and Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block. This paper includes the ﬁrst report of a positive fold test for Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block and improves the representative pole position in the Early Jurassic.

Most of the samples gave a characteristic remanent magnetization with unblocking temperatures up to 680 ◦C. The Lower Red Unit (LRU) is mainly composed of siltstones, sandstones, acidic tuffs and red volca - niclastic microconglomerates. In the Cadí Basin, these lithologies interfinger with pyroclastic rocks that contain ignimbrites and inter - bedded banded rhyolites. Finally, the Upper Red Unit (URU) contains red conglomerates, sandstones, and siltstones ( Fig. 1 G) with carbonate nodules, and lacustrine deposits. These rocks are arranged in two se - quences, with interbedded volcanic bodies at the bottom. Mafic minerals and plagioclases in the volcanic series are replaced by opaque minerals, chlorite, ferromagnesian silicates, carbonates and sericite ( Gisbert, 1981 ; Bixel, 1984 ). Radiometric dating of extrusive rocks of the GU in the Cadí Basin yielded Late Carboniferous ages, including 304.0 ± 1.5 Ma (andesite) and 300.4 ± 1.4 Ma (ignimbrite) ( Pereira et al., 2014 ). 3. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: ona, Spain ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Paleomagnetism Volcanic Red beds Late Carboniferous Permian Pyrenees ABSTRACT We have carried out a detailed paleomagnetic study of volcanic rocks (18 sites) and red beds (10 sites) from the Late-Carboniferous-Permian series of the Cadí Basin (Eastern Pyrenees). The study provides reliable Late Carboniferous-Permian paleomagnetic directions, in an area where paleomagnetic studies are scarce. The main characteristic component in both rock types shows a SSE direction with a shallow inclination and a dominant reverse polarity. The magnetic carriers, both in the volcanic rocks and the red beds, are magnetite and hematite. The main component is interpreted as a primary magnetization of Permian age in the red beds; in the Late Carboniferous volcanic rocks, the main component likely represents primary magnetization or early remagne - tization. These results are consistent with the poles for the Iberian plate during the Permian and indicate an absence of regional vertical axis rotations for the Orri nappe, in whose hanging wall the Cadí Basin was trans - ported southwards during the Pyrenean orogeny. 1. Introduction In spite of the difficulties in interpreting paleomagnetic directions in fold-and-thrust belts ( Pueyo et al., 2016a ), primary magnetizations can be used to unravel plate motions ( Gong et al., 2008 ; Vissers and Meijer, 2012 ) and thrust-related kinematics ( McCaig and McClelland, 1992 ; Oliva-Urcia and Pueyo, 2007 and 2019 ). In Iberia, the occurrence of widespread remagnetizations can preclude the use of paleomagnetic directions with such objectives. Nevertheless, secondary magnetizations may help to infer the deformational history of thrust belts and to obtain valuable kinematic information (e.g., Villalaín et al., 2016 ; Soto et al., 2008, 2011 ; Torres-L ´opez et al., 2018 ). netic directions with such objectives. Nevertheless, secondary magnetizations may help to infer the deformational history of thrust belts and to obtain valuable kinematic information (e.g., Villalaín et al., 2016 ; Soto et al., 2008, 2011 ; Torres-L ´opez et al., 2018 ). In the Pyrenees there are three remagnetization events, dated as Permian ( Pastor-Gal ´an et al., 2021 ), Early Cretaceous ( Larrasoa ˜na et al., 2003 ; Garc ´es et al., 2016 ) and Eocene-Oligocene ( Oliva-Urcia and Pueyo, 2007 ; Oliva-Urcia et al., 2008, 2012 ; Izquierdo-Lavall et al., 2015 ; Izquierdo-Llavall et al., 2018 ). These remagnetization events erased the primary magnetization of the rocks located within internal units of the orogen. Introduction In spite of the difficulties in interpreting paleomagnetic directions in fold-and-thrust belts ( Pueyo et al., 2016a ), primary magnetizations can be used to unravel plate motions ( Gong et al., 2008 ; Vissers and Meijer, 2012 ) and thrust-related kinematics ( McCaig and McClelland, 1992 ; Oliva-Urcia and Pueyo, 2007 and 2019 ). The Lower Red Unit (LRU) is mainly composed of siltstones, sandstones, acidic tuffs and red volca - niclastic microconglomerates. In the Cadí Basin, these lithologies interfinger with pyroclastic rocks that contain ignimbrites and inter - bedded banded rhyolites. Finally, the Upper Red Unit (URU) contains red conglomerates, sandstones, and siltstones ( Fig. 1 G) with carbonate nodules, and lacustrine deposits. These rocks are arranged in two se - quences, with interbedded volcanic bodies at the bottom. Mafic minerals and plagioclases in the volcanic series are replaced by opaque minerals, chlorite, ferromagnesian silicates, carbonates and sericite ( Gisbert, 1981 ; Bixel, 1984 ). Radiometric dating of extrusive rocks of the GU in the Cadí Basin yielded Late Carboniferous ages, including 304.0 ± 1.5 Ma (andesite) and 300.4 ± 1.4 Ma (ignimbrite) ( Pereira et al., 2014 ). 3. The main magnetic carriers of the magnetization in both lithologies are magnetite and hematite as observed in the results of the 3-axis IRM and the susceptibility-temperature curves. In the first experiment, the pres - ence of a high coercivity mineral, which points toward the presence of hematite in both lithologies, is clearly visible. In the susceptibility- temperature curves the decay for hematite is not visible, probably because magnetite has an intrinsic susceptibility of at least 10 3 – 10 4 times higher than hematite, while the multiplying factor for saturation remanence is only 50. In any case, the dominant reverse component shows a very low inclination after tectonic correction which is compatible with the primary reverse polarity magnetization retrieved for the Permian red beds. The high-temperature component of the volcanic rocks could also be primary in origin, but the similarity of the orientation of the paleo - magnetic vectors in relation to the red beds, in spite of their older age, points to a secondary origin of this magnetization. If the remagnetiza - tion is chemical in origin, as may be suggested by the strong, early alteration of minerals in the volcanic series ( Bixel, 1984 ), it should have occurred before the deposition of the overlying red beds. In this work, we focus on the Late Carboniferous-Permian Cadí Basin, which is a sector of the Pyrenees for which paleomagnetic data are relatively scarce ( Pueyo et al., 2016b and references therein). These basins have undergone significant transport in the hanging wall of one of the most important basement thrust sheets that define the Pyr - enean orogen (e.g. Gisbert, 1981 ). Palaeo- magnetic samples were collected at 40 sites from A (16 sites), B (16 sites) and C (8 sites) localities. In 36 of 40 sites, 18 pairs of successive sandstones and mudstones layers have been observed (Fig. 3). Location of each site was determined by portable naviga- tional system, whereas samples were oriented by magnetic compass. bserved in the Cretaceous red beds of the South China Block (SCB). Although, inclination shallowing has not been detected in the coastal area of the SCB (Morinaga & Liu 2004; Zhu et al. 2006), anomalously large shallowing has been reported from the Sichuan Basin of the same block (Otofuji et al . 1990; Enkin et al. 1991a). Following these observations, demand for further in- vestigations became high to trace local origin of the inclination shallowing. Small-scale variation of inclination shallowing can be observed in the red beds strata, which mainly depends on the distribution of the size of grains and their ﬂocculated matters (ﬂocs) in the hematite bearing sediments as well as their mechanical compaction (Payen & V erosub 1982; Tanet al. 2002; Heslop 2007; Mitra & Tauxe 2009). Accordingly, lithological variation on strata scale could be taken as one of the targets in studying inclination shallowing. Palaeomagnetic study of the red beds on lithological to locality scale can give us a clue to investigate the origin of inclination shallowing. As a ﬁrst step in this procedure, palaeomagnetic study have been conducted to detect grain size dependence of inclination shallowing. As a second step, locality-wise features of inclination shallowing in the southeast Asia are investigated. For this

directions of the remanent magne- tization (statistically) are preserved in the sandstone and mudstone layers. Grain size dependence of inclination variation in the red beds is still considered as controversial issue. In this connection three differ- ent approaches have been recognized; (1) no inclination shallowing in coarse-grained sediments but shallowing in clay-sized sediments; (2) no inclination shallowing in ﬁne-grain sediments but shallow- ing in coarse-grained sediments and (3) similar trend of inclination shallowing both in coarse and ﬁne-grained sediments. According to their experimental work, Tan et al . (2002) have claimed that hematite bearing clayey sediments underwent a compaction related inclination shallowing of 17 ◦–19◦, while coarse-grained sediments received very little inclination shallowing. Similar type of behaviour has been reported by Hodych & Hayatsu (1988) on the basis of their palaeomagnetic results from Jurassic red beds. Contrary to these views some of the researchers (Tucker 1979; Stamatakos et al . 1995; Tan et al . 2007) have observed that ﬁne-grained magnetic minerals, which carry magnetically hard component and distributed spectra of unblocking temperatures, have accurately recorded mag- netic ﬁeld directions without any inclination error. Because of their fragile nature, only small number of specimens could be prepared from several mud- stones layers, while no specimen could be obtained from site SB14. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) were measured with 2-G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer. At least one specimen from each sample was subjected to stepwise thermal demagneti- zation procedure up to 690 ◦C using Natsuhara TDS-1 thermal demagnetizer (with a residual ﬁeld of less than 5 nT). Results from demagnetization procedure were plotted on orthogonal vector dia- grams (Zijderveld 1967) to assess component structure as well as on equal-area projections to evaluate directional stability. Princi- pal component analysis (Kirschvink 1980) was used to estimate the component directions, and site-mean direction was calculated using Fisherian statistics (Fisher 1953). Progressive acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) was performed up to a maximum ﬁeld of 2.7 T using 2G-pulse magnetizer. Specimens with acquired IRM were then subjected to back ﬁeld demagnetization. To determine the unblocking tempera- ture spectra, thermal demagnetization of the composite IRMs (2.7, 0.4 and 0.12T along z, y and x axes of specimens, respectively) were carried out (Lowrie 1990). Received 2011 February 15; in original form 2010 August 24 SUMMARY Shallow palaeomagnetic inclinations have been frequently reported from the red beds of central and southeast Asia. To trace the origin of this phenomenon, inclination variation in southeast Asia is examined on lithological to locality scale. Lithological aspect of this variation has been studied using the Early Cretaceous Bailong and Cangxi formations of the Bazhong area (32.1 ◦N, 106.7◦E), the northern Sichuan Basin. Samples from 36 sites, consisting 18 pairs of successive sandstones and mudstones layers, were collected for this purpose from a syn- clinal structure. Stepwise thermal demagnetization of most samples revealed the presence of stable characteristic remanent magnetization, which is generally unblocked by 680 ◦C. Early Cretaceous Bailong and Cangxi formations of the Bazhong area (32.1 ◦N, 106.7◦E), the northern Sichuan Basin. Samples from 36 sites, consisting 18 pairs of successive sandstones and mudstones layers, were collected for this purpose from a syn- clinal structure. Stepwise thermal demagnetization of most samples revealed the presence of stable characteristic remanent magnetization, which is generally unblocked by 680 ◦C. Pos- itive fold and reversal tests suggest a primary origin for this component, yielding the Early Cretaceous palaeomagnetic direction of declination/inclination = 20.9 ◦/26.5◦ (ks = 37.2, α95 = 4.4◦, N = 30). 10 pairs of sandstone and mudstone layers show almost identical incli- nations (I sandstones = 23.3◦ ± 3.7◦ and Imudstones = 24.7◦ ± 2.4◦), but 27 ◦ shallower than that expected from the Eurasian apparent polar wander paths (APWPs), indicating that no litho- logical variation in inclination has occurred. Location-wise variation in inclination shallowing is examined through palaeomagnetic data from Late Jurassic to Eocene red beds distributed around southeast Asia.
